name: Type IIx fibre (fast glycolytic)
short_description: The largest-diameter, fastest, most purely glycolytic fibre in human skeletal muscle: a single, unbranched, cylindrical cell centimetres long and ~70 um across, cross-striated along its whole length, with many flattened nuclei just under the sarcolemma at the periphery (never one central nucleus), sparse mitochondria, a thin capillary supply and abundant glycogen granules, pale pink-cream rather than red. What older histochemistry called human 'Type IIb' is this fibre under a different name -- true MYH4-expressing IIb is a rodent fibre, essentially absent from adult human limb muscle.

textbook.1: partial (gemini-2.5-flash-image; correct science on first try -- pale pink-cream unbranched cylinder, continuous A/I banding, 10+ peripheral nuclei visibly hugging the rim including 4 arranged around the rim of the end-cap disc (none central), sparse individually-scattered mitochondria-like ovals, abundant small glycogen dots, thin external capillary. FAIL on framing: both ends of the fibre show a complete closed end-cap disc fully inside the canvas -- the 'short stubby sausage that fits inside the frame' failure the brief calls out, even though the length:width ratio (~4:1) keeps it from reading as literally stubby. Fix-prompt: force both ends to be cropped by the canvas edge.
textbook.2: partial (gemini-2.5-flash-image; framing improved -- one end now cropped by the frame, the other still a closed disc -- but the capillary rendered as an alternating red/white segmented rod (candy-cane / swab-stick pattern), a biologically wrong, faintly manufactured-looking artefact. Fix-prompt: capillary must be a single continuous crimson tone, no stripes/segments.
textbook.3: DISPROVEN, do not trust this entry. Originally recorded as 'pass' and used as final -- that was wrong on two counts, found by orchestrator review with a magnified centre crop (a check this agent never ran): (a) the whole surface pattern is fine PINK/CREAM STRIPES RUNNING LENGTHWISE (parallel to the fibre's long axis, i.e. myofibrils seen lengthwise) with NO transverse A/I cross-striation anywhere -- the defining visible feature of a skeletal muscle fibre was simply absent, even though this entry's own text claimed 'continuous A/I banding'; (b) BOTH ends show a closed, fully-enclosed rounded cap sitting entirely inside the canvas (confirmed by cropping and magnifying both corners) -- not 'one end cropped, one end capped' as originally logged. The fine longitudinal myofibril texture is visually convincing enough at full-frame scale to be mistaken for cross-striation at a glance; a zoomed centre crop is required to tell them apart. Capillary, nuclei, mitochondria and glycogen claims in the original text were accurate. Superseded by attempt 4 below.
textbook.4: pass (gemini-3-pro-image; escalated straight to the pro tier per the model ladder's 'already paid the two-fails toll' rule, and using corrected positive-direction phrasing for the striation ('regular narrow dark and light bands running across the fibre, perpendicular to its length, repeating evenly end to end like rungs on a ladder, with the fine myofibrils running lengthwise underneath') plus a stronger corner-fill framing check borrowed from the type-i-fibre exemplar. Came back correct on the FIRST pro-tier attempt. Verified by magnified 30% centre crop (per SKILL.md -- FFT/line-sample tests do not discriminate this failure): fine slate Z-disc lines cross the fibre in register at regular intervals, alternating darker dusty-rose A-band dashes and pale cream I-band gaps run the full visible length, AND fine lengthwise myofibril striping is visible underneath/within each transverse band -- both patterns present simultaneously, as real anatomy requires. Framing re-verified by cropping and enlarging both opposite corners: fibre body colour (striped pink-cream) fills both corners edge-to-edge with no background triangle and no rounded end-cap visible at either end -- the fibre now genuinely runs out of frame at both ends, not one. >=7 peripheral nuclei counted, all on the rim, none central. Mitochondria sparse and individually scattered (not dense rows). Glycogen granules abundant, small, gold-tan. Capillary a single smooth continuous crimson curve, no stripe artefact. No baked text found. No border on any of the 4 edges (dark charcoal fill reaches every edge). Used as final; 10-label SVG rebuilt against this new base image and every anchor re-verified by direct pixel sampling against the raw render (not just the rasterised SVG, whose leader lines can occlude the exact anchor pixel).

sem.1: partial (gemini-2.5-flash-image; surface-only false-colour SEM, correct pale pink-cream tone, small oval bulges at the rim plausibly reading as sub-surface peripheral nuclei -- but the fibre sits as a short capped segment fully on a bounded pale rectangular slab, both ends visible, reading closer to the 'stubby sausage' failure than the other styles' attempt 1s. The 'regular ribbing' described in this entry at the time was, on later re-inspection, oriented lengthwise (parallel to the tube), not transverse -- this was not caught at the time.
sem.2: DISPROVEN, do not trust this entry. Originally recorded as 'pass' and used as final. Orchestrator review with a magnified crop found the surface ribbing runs LENGTHWISE along the fibre (a fine longitudinal corduroy texture, i.e. myofibril grain seen from outside), not transverse rings around the tube as the entry's own text claimed ('corduroy-like transverse ribbing'). The fibre does run off both edges correctly -- that part of the original claim held up. Superseded by attempt 3 below.
sem.3: pass (gemini-3-pro-image; escalated to the pro tier with corrected positive-direction phrasing for the surface ribbing ('fine, closely-spaced ridges that encircle the fibre like the rings on a drinking straw or the rungs of a ladder laid crosswise over a rope, perpendicular to its long axis'). Came back correct on the FIRST pro-tier attempt. Verified by magnified centre crop: many fine ridges wrap around the tube's circumference, perpendicular to the long axis, evenly spaced the entire visible length -- true transverse banding, not lengthwise grain. Long shallow oval bulges visible along both flanks at the rim, consistent with peripheral nuclei pushing up against the sarcolemma from inside (the only way a surface-only SEM technique can honestly gesture at nuclear position). Pale dusty pink-cream false colour (not deep red, not grey). Framing re-verified at both opposite corners: fibre substrate/body fills each corner edge-to-edge, no closed end visible at either tip. No baked text. No border. Single dominant specimen. Used as final. Surface-only per the SEM medium, so -- per project convention -- no labelled SVG is built for this style (interior structures like bands/Z-disc/mitochondria/glycogen are not visible in a genuine SEM anyway).

reference: pass (2026-08-21). Wikimedia Commons 'Skeletal muscle - longitudinal section.jpg' (LM, H&E, Dept. of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College), CC BY-SA 3.0/GFDL. Viewed at full resolution and in two magnified crops: several diagonal fibres show unmistakable fine, continuous cross-striation along their whole visible length -- the single most important checkable fact for this subject. No baked-in text, scale bar, border or watermark; used as downloaded, no cleaning needed (edit_image.py skipped -- nothing to remove). Honest caveats recorded in full in the render.md: (1) one or two darker elongated profiles sit at fibre/septum boundaries consistent with a peripheral nucleus, but are not sharp/numerous enough in this specific plate to *count* with the confidence the render checklist demands -- this reference earns its place on striations, not on a countable nuclear tally; (2) H&E does not distinguish fibre type at all, so this plate cannot show which fibres are IIx versus I or IIa -- two differential-stain candidates (a human ATPase pH4.0 checkerboard and a human ATPase pH4.3 case) were found and are named in the log, but both were pathological specimens and single-pH ATPase only separates Type I from Type II as a group, not IIa from IIx, so neither was used as the primary reference.
